analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to residents who buy in, and requires Medicaid to cover reproductive care including abortion.
analysis.headline: The State Public Option Act, introduced by Sen. Schatz with 14 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let each state decide whether to open its Medicaid program to any resident who wants to pay in, with premiums capped at 8.5% of family income and federal help paying them. It would also give the generous federal matching rate to any state that expands Medicaid, whenever it expands, and require every state's Medicaid program to cover reproductive health care, including abortion. It never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, uninsured adults who earn too much for Medicaid but can't afford private plans would gain access to a low-cost public plan, with premiums capped at 8.5% of income and federal tax credits usable toward them. People in the ten states that never expanded Medicaid could gain full Medicaid coverage with the enhanced federal match. Medicaid enrollees nationwide would gain guaranteed coverage of comprehensive reproductive care, including abortion. Primary care providers serving Medicaid patients would get higher payment rates.

how_it_helps.text: Lets uninsured or underinsured people buy into their state Medicaid plan starting in 2026, with premiums capped at 8.5% of family income and standard limits on deductibles and copays.
Buy-in enrollees can use their ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions toward the Medicaid plan, and can enroll through the ACA exchanges.
Gives every state that expands Medicaid the enhanced 90% federal matching rate whenever it expands, not just states that expanded by 2014, removing the financial penalty for late expansion.
Requires Medicaid in every state to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care, including abortion services, effective January 1, 2026.

Restores and expands the enhanced federal payment floor for primary care in Medicaid, covering more provider types (including nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and certified nurse-midwives), so doctors are paid more to see Medicaid patients.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would pay a 90% share of the buy-in program's administrative costs and enhanced matching rates for expansion, ultimately borne by taxpayers. Private insurers selling individual-market plans would lose customers to the cheaper public plan. States that opt in would administer the program and share premium revenue risk; federal taxpayers would also fund the higher primary care payment floor.

drawbacks.text: Participation is entirely optional for states: the bill only creates the option, so residents of states that decline to act get nothing, which could leave coverage uneven by geography.

The bill spends substantial federal money: a 90% federal match for buy-in administration, enhanced matching rates for all expansion states, and a permanent federal payment floor for primary care in Medicaid, adding to federal health outlays.
The reproductive health provision requires every state Medicaid program to cover abortion services, which is a significant federal preemption of state policy and the bill's most contested provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real: a low-cost public insurance option for uninsured and poorly-insured Americans, expanded Medicaid federal funding for holdout states, mandated abortion coverage, and higher primary care payment rates in Medicaid. The costs are correspondingly large: large new federal health spending, states must act before anything happens, and the mandate that state Medicaid programs cover abortion services (using federal funds in effect) is the single most likely flashpoint for a Senate requiring 60 votes. The bill would also shrink the private individual insurance market's customer base, which the industry would call unfair competition with a government plan.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to its Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it went nowhere.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 12, 2025 and, the same day, read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The complete action history contains no further actions: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion action through the end of the recorded history.
The bill's support was limited to its sponsor and 14 Democratic cosponsors; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers and opponents of a public option and of federal abortion-coverage mandates benefit from the bill's inaction; uninsured people in expansion-waiting states gained nothing.

for.name: 14 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Lujan, Merkley, Shaheen, Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Klobuchar, Welch, Rosen, Smith, Murphy, Booker, Durbin, and Heinrich.

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 Senate supporters are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-held Finance Committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill creates a government-run plan that competes directly with private individual-market insurers, and it could draw away customers, especially where premiums are high. Some insurers would also lose the mandatory Medicaid managed-care roles to state-run coverage.
Medicaid typically pays some of the lowest drug prices of any payer; a Medicaid-based public option channeling more patients into those rates would put downward pressure on drug revenue.

industries.industry: Primary care physicians, nurse practitioners, and community clinics
industries.note: The bill guarantees Medicaid pays primary care at Medicare rates and extends the payment floor to nurse practitioners, physician assistants, midwives, and rural health clinics, increasing revenue for front-line providers.

States get a 90% federal match for running the buy-in program and new federal implementation funds, but they must shoulder administration of a new population and the federal abortion-coverage mandate constrains state discretion.

analysis.trajectory: With only 14 of 45 Senate Democrats on board, no Republican support, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee showing no activity, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or vote in the 119th Congress; the most likely path is expiration at the end of the Congress, with possible reintroduction later.
